page_hint: Ch 22, §8 mini-case, 'The peak, not the average' paragraph
quoted_clause: a homogeneous cluster sized at ~16 hosts clears both budgets
observed: The same paragraph calculates ~16.3 hosts at 40% MFU as needed for prefill at the 40 rps peak. 16 hosts × 3.164 PFLOPS/host = 50.62 PFLOPS, which is less than the 51.52 PFLOP/s required. 16 hosts would NOT clear the prefill budget; 17 hosts would (17 × 3.164 = 53.79 > 51.52).
correction: Change '~16 hosts' to '~17 hosts' (or 'at least 17 hosts') to be consistent with the ~16.3 calculation in the same paragraph.
acceptance_test: Verify that the stated host count × 3.164 PFLOPS/host ≥ 51.52 PFLOP/s.
verdict_evidence: chapter-22/chapter-22.md:148 computes '40 × 1.288 ≈ 51.5 PFLOP/s ... ~16.3 hosts at 40% MFU (7.91 × 0.4 = 3.16 PFLOPS/host)' and then says 'a homogeneous cluster sized at ~16 hosts clears both budgets'. Recomputed: 16 × 3.164 = 50.62 PFLOPS < 51.5 needed (short by ~0.9 PFLOPS); 16.3 × 3.164 = 51.57, so a sufficiency claim must round up to 17.
fix_instruction: At chapter-22/chapter-22.md:148 change '~16 hosts' to '~17 hosts (16.3 at 40% MFU, rounded up)'.

page_hint: Ch 22, §7 What We Still Don't Know, second loop-specific bullet
quoted_clause: so the loop's ranking of the two bottlenecks can flip without any change in traffic
observed: The claim is imprecise about what 'ranking' means. If it means the classification (prefill = compute-bound, decode = bandwidth-bound), the claim is wrong: prefill arithmetic intensity ≈ L FLOP/byte and decode arithmetic intensity ≈ 1 FLOP/byte are both independent of parameter count N, so the classification does not change with model size. If it means which resource is more binding in absolute terms, the claim may be valid but is not what the sentence says.
correction: Reword to distinguish the two senses: e.g., 'the relative magnitude of the KV-capacity term versus the compute and bandwidth terms can shift, changing which resource is the binding constraint, even though the prefill-compute and decode-bandwidth classifications themselves are unchanged.'
acceptance_test: A reader should be able to state whether the compute-bound/bandwidth-bound classification changes with model size (it does not) and whether the relative binding constraint can change (it can).
verdict_evidence: ch22 L139 says the KV term's N-insensitivity means 'the loop's ranking of the two bottlenecks can flip'; the chapter's two bottlenecks are prefill-compute and decode-bandwidth (L101-103), and both scale as 2N·I/FLOPS and 2N·O/BW, so their ratio is N-independent and cannot flip with model size at fixed traffic.
fix_instruction: Reword to distinguish the senses: '…so the relative weight of the compute/bandwidth terms versus the KV-capacity term can shift the binding constraint, even though the prefill-compute and decode-bandwidth classifications themselves are unchanged.'

page_hint: Ch 22, §7 What We Still Don't Know, second loop-specific bullet
quoted_clause: moves the 2NL prefill term and the ~140 GB weight read in the same direction but not the KV-cache term
observed: The phrase 'not the KV-cache term' is ambiguous: it can be read as 'the KV cache does not change' (incorrect — a smaller model has fewer layers and smaller hidden dimension, so KV cache per token decreases) or as 'the KV cache does not change in the same proportion as parameter count' (correct). The subsequent clause 'which depends on context length and layer count rather than parameter count' clarifies intent but does not resolve the grammatical ambiguity of 'not.'
correction: Reword to: 'moves the 2NL prefill term and the ~140 GB weight read in proportion to parameter count, but the KV-cache term moves by a different proportion, because it depends on context length and layer count rather than scaling linearly with parameter count.'
acceptance_test: A reader should state that the KV cache decreases when the model shrinks, but not in the same proportion as parameter count.
verdict_evidence: ch22 L139 'moves the 2NL prefill term and the ~140 GB weight read in the same direction but not the KV-cache term' reads as 'the KV term does not move', which is false — KV/token = 2·layers·hidden·bytes falls with model size (70B: 80×8192 ≈ 2.62 MB/token at 2 bytes; a 32-layer 4096-hidden model ≈ 0.52 MB/token), just not in proportion to parameter count.
fix_instruction: Reword: '…moves the 2NL prefill term and the ~140 GB weight read roughly in proportion to parameter count, but the KV-cache term by a different proportion, because it scales with layer count × hidden size rather than with parameters.'

page_hint: Ch 22, §7 What We Still Don't Know, mechanism-layer bullet 4
quoted_clause: HBM3e and MI300X publish higher peaks
observed: MI300X uses HBM3 (not HBM3e). Grouping 'HBM3e' with 'MI300X' in a single noun phrase implies MI300X uses HBM3e, which is incorrect. MI325X is the MI300-series part that uses HBM3E.
correction: Reword to 'HBM3e parts (e.g., H200) and the MI300X publish higher peaks' or 'newer parts with HBM3e and the MI300X with HBM3 publish higher peaks.'
acceptance_test: Verify that each product named is associated with its correct memory technology.
verdict_evidence: ch22 L134 'HBM3e and MI300X publish higher peaks' groups a memory class with a GPU; the book's own ch2 L158 rule is 'name the SKU, not the memory class', where H200 is the HBM3e part (4.8 TB/s) and 'AMD MI300X is ~5.3 TB/s' is listed separately (MI300X is HBM3; the HBM3E part is MI325X).
fix_instruction: Reword: 'HBM3e parts (e.g. H200) and the MI300X (HBM3, ~5.3 TB/s) publish higher peaks …'.

page_hint: Ch 22 §3, 'The loop on a second workload'
quoted_clause: KV footprint per request is 2.62 MB × 400 ≈ 1.05 GB rather than ~24.1 GB
observed: For the stated 400-input/900-output workload, the KV cache at end of turn is 2.62 MB × (400+900) ≈ 3.41 GB, not 1.05 GB. The canonical table uses 9.5K max for 9.2K input + 300 output, so the second workload uses an inconsistent prompt-only basis.
correction: Use 2.62 MB × 1,300 ≈ 3.41 GB for max KV, or label 1.05 GB as prompt-only and compare it to 24.1 GB prompt-only.
acceptance_test: Both workloads use the same KV basis; recomputation from 400+900 and 9,200+300 matches the printed values.
verdict_evidence: chapter-22/chapter-22.md:67 gives the second workload as ~400 input + ~900 output and then states 'the KV footprint per request is 2.62 MB x 400 ≈ 1.05 GB rather than ~24.1 GB'. End-of-turn residency is 2.62 MB x 1,300 = 3.41 GB; the 24.1 GB comparator is the 9.2K prompt-only figure while the canonical table uses the 9.5K max (24.9 GB). Mixed bases.
fix_instruction: At chapter-22/chapter-22.md:67 write 'the prompt-only KV at 400 tokens is 2.62 MB x 400 ≈ 1.05 GB (≈3.41 GB at the end-of-turn 1,300 tokens), against ~24.1 GB prompt-only / ~24.9 GB end-of-turn for the canonical 9.2K/9.5K request'.

quoted_clause: the 2 × params × tokens approximation may ignore activation reuse across batched requests
observed: Independent requests in a batch do not share activations; batching improves hardware utilization, not FLOP count. The 2NL approximation is not invalidated by cross-request activation reuse.
correction: Remove 'activation reuse across batched requests'; if discussing corrections, refer to kernel overhead, padding, or activation memory, not cross-request reuse.
acceptance_test: No claim of cross-request activation reuse; batching is described as utilization/efficiency, not FLOP reduction.
verdict_evidence: ch02 l.166 (the cited §7) states continuous batching 'does not reuse one request's transformer activations ... so it does not reduce the mathematical FLOP count per request', directly contradicting ch22 l.132's 'may ignore activation reuse across batched requests'; ch04 l.249 likewise assigns prefix reuse to prefix caching, 'not to continuous batching'.
fix_instruction: Rewrite ch22 l.132: '**Achieved prefill efficiency under continuous batching** - Chapter 2 §7; 2 x params x tokens is exact per token and batching does not change it, but sustained MFU does, and it swings the canonical prefill host count from ~1.6 (100% of peak) to ~4.1 (40% MFU) at average load.'

quoted_clause: If prefill needs FLOPS and decode needs bandwidth, a single homogeneous GPU pool is suboptimal.
observed: The text later says P/D disaggregation depends on utilization, duplicated residency, KV-transfer cost, topology, workload shape, and burstiness. The unqualified 'is suboptimal' contradicts those caveats and overstates the case.
correction: Change to 'can be suboptimal' or 'may leave performance on the table'; keep the later measurement caveats.
acceptance_test: The claim is qualified and consistent with the subsequent list of dependencies.
verdict_evidence: chapter-22/chapter-22.md:103 asserts 'a single homogeneous GPU pool is suboptimal', then two sentences later says whether disaggregation 'needs fewer GPUs ... depends on achievable utilization, duplicated model residency, KV-transfer cost, interconnect topology, workload shape, burstiness ... those effects must be measured'. The unqualified 'is suboptimal' overstates a conclusion the same paragraph says is unmeasured.
fix_instruction: At chapter-22/chapter-22.md:103 change to 'a single homogeneous GPU pool can be suboptimal', keeping the later measurement caveats.

quoted_clause: this 30× ratio pushes the design toward high prefill compute and KV-capacity pressure
observed: KV capacity is driven by absolute context length and model architecture, not by the input/output ratio. A 9.2K/9.2K workload has ratio 1 but the same KV capacity as 9.2K/300 at the same total context.
correction: Attribute KV pressure to the 9.2K context length; use the 30× ratio only for prefill/decode balance.
acceptance_test: The sentence separates ratio effects from absolute-context effects; a counterexample with ratio 1 and the same context is not contradicted.
verdict_evidence: Line 148 asserts 'a homogeneous cluster sized at ~16 hosts clears both budgets' with only the prefill derivation (51.5 PFLOP/s / 3.16 PFLOPS = 16.3 hosts) shown; a KV check with the chapter's own 24.1 GB/request and Ch 17's 436 GB KV budget (640 - 140 - 64) gives 18.1 requests/host and needs ~19 hosts for the 343 in-flight at 40 rps, so 16 is short.
fix_instruction: Add the KV arithmetic to the mini-case (436 GB KV budget / 24.1 GB = ~18 requests/host, 40 rps x 8.58 s = ~343 in flight -> ~19 hosts) and restate the conclusion as '~16-19 hosts, prefill- or KV-bound depending on the KV budget, with 21 hosts carrying the margin'.

quoted_clause: moves the 2NL prefill term and the ~140 GB weight read in the same direction but not the KV-cache term, which depends on context length and layer count rather than parameter count
observed: A smaller dense model may have fewer layers or KV heads, so the KV-cache term can also shrink. Saying it does not move is misleading; it depends on layer count, KV-head count, head dimension, precision, and context length.
correction: Say the KV term depends on layer/KV-head geometry and context length and may or may not shrink with a smaller model; it is not tied to parameter count alone.
acceptance_test: The text acknowledges possible KV change when the model is replaced and lists the governing architecture variables.
verdict_evidence: ch22 l.139 says a model swap moves 2NL and the ~140 GB read 'but not the KV-cache term, which depends on context length and layer count' - layer and KV-head count are exactly what shrink with model size (canonical 2.62 MB/token = 2 x 80 layers x 64 KV heads x 128 x 2 B), so the KV term does move.
fix_instruction: Rewrite ch22 l.139 so the KV term moves too but by a different factor (it scales with layer/KV-head count and context length rather than parameter count), preserving the 'ranking can flip' conclusion.
